nutshell: Lifelong person ReID (LReID) methods cram knowledge from a growing sequence of domains into one fixed-capacity model, causing catastrophic forgetting. VIA instead dynamically expands a CLIP-ReID backbone with per-domain LoRA expert adapters (UnA), a shared adapter pool with learned routing for cross-domain knowledge reuse (DAD), a similarity-based learning-rate decay that protects generalizable encoder knowledge as more domains arrive (HDC), and a training-free, statistics-based inference-time router (SGAS) that picks the right adapters for a test sample without domain labels.
contributions: Unseen-domain Person Adapter (UnA): a per-domain pair of cascaded LoRA adapters embedded inside the MLP block (before and after the GELU nonlinearity) rather than in parallel with MLP/attention as prior adapter-insertion strategies do, giving each domain isolated, deeply-integrated capacity.

Domain-aware Dispatch (DAD): a shared pool of LoRA experts with a per-domain top-k router (Eq. 4-5), plus a pairwise-orthogonality decoupling loss on the experts' low-rank factors (Eq. 6) to reduce redundant shared knowledge, and a domain-aware router initialization that copies the router of the most similar previously-seen domain (via 2-Wasserstein feature-distribution similarity) instead of random init.

Holistic Domain Controller (HDC): decays the image encoder's initial learning rate for each new domain as a function of both average similarity to prior domains and how many domains have been seen so far (Eq. 9), to protect accumulated domain-invariant knowledge without freezing the encoder outright.

Similarity-Guided Auto-Selector (SGAS): at inference, routes a test sample to the adapter set of whichever seen domain its features are statistically closest to (Eq. 10-12, same Wasserstein-distance similarity used for router init), with no domain classifier or domain label needed.
deficiencies: The paper's headline SOTA comparisons (Table 1/2, Section 4.3, e.g. 'VIA attains 79.9% mAP... clearly outperforming DASK (58.5%)') are confounded by a backbone/baseline switch, not just the proposed modules: the paper's own 'Baseline' row (plain CLIP-ReID, no UnA/DAD/HDC/SGAS at all) already scores 66.4/78.1 seen-avg mAP/R@1 on Order-1 - roughly 11 points above the best prior SOTA (DASK, 55.4/69.3) - before any of VIA's actual contributions are added. The fair, backbone-controlled comparison is Table 3 (Baseline 66.4/78.1 -> full VIA 77.7/86.6, +11.3/+8.5), which is a real but much smaller gain than the ~20+ point gaps emphasized in the SOTA comparison section.

Table 3's own ablation shows adding UnA alone (the paper's core, most-emphasized module) actually *collapses* unseen-domain generalization versus the plain baseline - from 73.1/66.5 mAP/R@1 down to 61.8/55.1, an 11+ point drop - because isolating each domain's knowledge into private adapters removes whatever cross-domain sharing let the baseline generalize. Section 4.4's discussion of the UnA row only reports the seen-domain gains ('3.4% and 5.5% improvements') and never mentions this unseen-domain regression; DAD is what recovers it, but that dependency isn't flagged as a limitation of UnA in isolation.

Similarly, Table 3's DAD-without-UnA row (shared adapters only) actually performs *worse* than the plain baseline on seen domains (57.6/70.7 vs. baseline's 66.4/78.1, an 8.8/7.4-point drop) - a result the ablation narrative in Section 4.4 never discusses, since the text only ever compares 'DAD on top of UnA' against 'UnA alone,' silently skipping the row where DAD alone underperforms doing nothing.

All reported numbers across every table are single-run point estimates (no variance/seeds/confidence intervals), and several of the module-choice ablations used to justify design decisions (Table 5's router-transfer comparison, Table 6's learning-rate strategy comparison) have sub-1-to-2-point margins between the winning and losing variants - within plausible run-to-run noise that isn't checked.

The overhead analysis (Table 7, Section 4.6) reports a per-domain cost (+11M params, +291M GPU memory, +39M storage) that is framed as 'acceptable,' but this cost is cumulative and linear in the number of domains, and the LReID benchmark used here only chains 5 training domains - the framework's core selling point (dynamic expansion) is never stress-tested at the domain counts (dozens+) where a truly 'lifelong' deployment would actually strain this linear growth.
notable: SGAS's test-time routing is genuinely training-free: it reuses the same Wasserstein-distance domain-similarity statistics computed for router initialization (Eq. 10) to route unlabeled test samples to the nearest seen domain's adapters at inference, with no auxiliary domain classifier - a clean, reusable pattern for other modular/MoE-style continual learning setups that need domain-agnostic expert selection. Also notable: the domain-similarity statistics (mean/covariance for the Wasserstein distance, Eq. 10-11) are computed using features from an off-the-shelf Inception-V3 network, not the CLIP-ViT backbone the rest of the pipeline is built on - an inconsistency in the implementation that isn't explained (e.g. why not reuse CLIP image features already being computed).
